conceptual_foundation.introduction: Introduces geometry and angles through the physical experience of turning and rotation, utilizing clock hands, paper fans, straw angle testers, and compass directions.

core_concepts.concept: Angle as a Degree of Turn
core_concepts.explanation: An angle measures the amount of rotation between two rays sharing a common endpoint (vertex) or the degree of turn from a fixed direction.
core_concepts.example: Turning a door handle or turning clock hands from 12 to 3 creates an angle.

core_concepts.explanation: A complete circular rotation is a full turn. A quarter (1/4) turn forms a Right Angle (90°).
core_concepts.example: Moving clock hands from 12 to 3 is a 1/4 turn, forming an exact right angle (L-shape).

core_concepts.explanation: Angles are classified based on their turn relative to a right angle (1/4 turn) and a straight angle (1/2 turn): Acute Angle (< 1/4 turn), Right Angle (= 1/4 turn), Obtuse Angle (between 1/4 and 1/2 turn), Straight Angle (= 1/2 turn).
core_concepts.example: The angle between scissors blades opened slightly is acute; fully stretched arms form a straight angle.

core_concepts.explanation: Clockwise moves in the direction of clock hands (12 -> 3 -> 6 -> 9 -> 12). Anti-clockwise moves in the opposite direction (12 -> 9 -> 6 -> 3 -> 12).
core_concepts.example: Turning a screw right is clockwise; turning left is anti-clockwise.

core_concepts.explanation: Navigating four main compass directions: North (N), East (E), South (S), West (W). Facing North and making a 1/4 turn clockwise leads to East.
core_concepts.example: Facing North, a 1/2 turn brings you to face South.

key_formulas_and_rules: Acute Angle < 1/4 Turn < Obtuse Angle < 1/2 Turn
real_world_applications: Navigation, reading clock time, yoga postures, structural engineering, and sports motion analysis.
